narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'not afraid of many thousands' and the type (102) is affect: an emotional posture, not a mere event. No source (103 absent) is named for the fearlessness within the verse itself, and no seat (104 none) is given — the refusal of fear is not lodged in a single organ but held as a whole-self state (locus 116 internal:ib-state). The bearer (105) is the psalmist, and the operation (106) is a deliberate act of the self: it declares it will not fear even ten thousands ranged against it, fear refused on the ground of God's sustaining. The target (107) is fearlessness itself and the coupling (112) is 'not-afraid' — the two describe one resolved interior. Manner (108) is marked none, intensity (109), specifier (110) and effect (111) are all absent, and no prohibition (113) attaches: the fearlessness is simply asserted, not commanded or forbidden. The discovery (114) fixes it at v6 — the numbers that should terrify are faced down by trust. Role (115) is characteristic: this is a stable trait of the inner being, courage generated not by the size of the threat but by confidence that God upholds the sleeper who wakes again.
narratives.story: Surrounded by thousands who have turned against him, the psalmist makes a plain decision inside himself: he will not be afraid. This is not a passing flicker but a settled state of the whole person — you cannot point to one part of him where the courage sits; it fills all of him. Nothing in the verse says the fear rushes in and is beaten back; he simply names the enemy's overwhelming numbers and refuses to let them frighten him. The refusal has no particular degree, no bodily trigger, no spelled-out consequence — just a steady, chosen fearlessness resting on the trust that the God who let him sleep and wake will keep him.
narratives.variation_note: Unlike the terror readings of this word elsewhere, and unlike the reverent 'fear of the LORD', #1 is deliberate, chosen fearlessness (locus internal:ib-state) grounded in God's personal sustaining of the psalmist — courage against human numbers, not dread and not worship.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'enter to bow in the fear of God' and the type (102) is affect. No source (103 absent) is separately tagged and no seat (104 none) is given — the reverent approach is a whole-self posture (locus 116 internal:ib-state), not an organ's act. The bearer (105) is the psalmist; the operation (106) is the decisive movement: borne by God's steadfast love, the self enters the house and bows toward the temple in reverent fear. The target (107) is reverent-worship and the coupling (112) is 'bow-in-fear' — approach and awe are one motion. Manner (108) is none; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) are absent; no prohibition (113) attaches. The discovery (114) at v7 makes the ground explicit: the interior does not approach on its own merit but on the abundance of God's love, and the posture in which it arrives is fear. Role (115) is characteristic. The process runs from God's love (the enabling ground) through the self's entering and bowing to a settled reverence — awe here is not paralysis but the very form worship takes.
narratives.story: Because God's love is so abundant, the psalmist dares to come into God's house and bow low toward the holy temple — and the mood in which he comes is fear. It is not dread that keeps him out but reverence that shapes how he goes in; entering and bowing are a single act of awe. He does not lean on his own goodness to justify the approach; the love shown to him is what lets him come at all. This reverent worship is not felt in one part of him but is the whole man's posture, a steady reverence rather than a momentary shudder.
narratives.variation_note: This first reading of 'enter' is reverent approach to worship, awe as the shape of coming near (target reverent-worship); it contrasts with #2 (Psa 143:2), where the same word turns to a plea NOT to be entered into judgment — worship-approach here versus dread of a verdict there.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'honours the God-fearers' and the type (102) is affect — an inner valuing. No source (103 absent) is tagged and no seat (104 none) is named: this reordered esteem is a whole-self disposition (locus 116 internal:ib-state), not an organ's function. The bearer (105) is the righteous person of Psalm 15; the operation (106) is a double movement of esteem — in his eyes a vile person is despised, but he honours those who fear the LORD, valuing people by God's standard rather than by status or power. The target (107) is right-valuation and the coupling (112) is 'honour-God-fearers'. Manner (108) is none; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent; no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) at v4 names it as a reordered approval: the interior's likes and dislikes track God's own. Role (115) is characteristic. The inner-being process here is evaluative — the human esteem-faculty is retuned so that reverence for God, not worldly rank, decides whom the self honours.
narratives.story: The person who may dwell with God is one whose inner scale of worth has been reset: he looks down on the worthless and lifts up those who genuinely fear God. His approval no longer follows money or power but goes to the people God values. This is a settled trait of the whole man, not a mood that comes and goes and not tied to any single feeling in the body. What he admires and what he scorns line up with what God admires and scorns.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'the fear of the LORD, clean' and the type (102) is affect. No source (103 absent) is separately tagged; no seat (104 none) is given — reverent fear is held as a whole-self state (locus 116 internal:ib-state). The bearer (105) is the psalmist; the operation (106) names reverent fear itself as a pure and permanent interior posture: the fear of the LORD is clean, enduring forever. The target (107) is reverent-fear and the coupling (112) is 'clean-fear'. Manner (108) none; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent; no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) at v9 contrasts this fear with defiling fears: unlike the dreads that stain, this one is pure and lasts. Role (115) is characteristic. Set among the perfect law, sure testimony and right precepts, this reverence is treated as one of God's clean gifts to the inner life — a fear that purifies rather than corrupts, and that does not expire.
narratives.story: Listed beside God's perfect law and trustworthy word, the fear of the LORD is called clean and unending. This is the kind of fear that does not soil a person but keeps them pure, and it never wears out. It is not a jolt in the body but a lasting attitude of the whole self. Against every fear that darkens and defiles, this one is spotless and permanent.
narratives.variation_note: Reading #1 of this reverence-word treats the fear of the LORD as itself clean and eternal — a static, praised quality; #2 (Psa 55:5) uses the same word for raw terror flooding in, and #3 (Psa 90:11), #4 (Psa 111:10), #5 (Psa 119:38) as reverence owed, wisdom's beginning, and the aim of the confirmed promise. This one is fear described as a pure possession.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'summon the God-fearers to praise' and — distinctively — the type (102) is volition, an act of the will rather than a bare affect. No source (103 absent); no seat (104 none) — the summons issues from the whole rescued self (locus 116 internal:ib-state). The bearer (105) is 'those who fear the LORD', the community addressed; the operation (106) is the self, delivered, calling all who fear the LORD to praise, glorify and stand in awe of him, drawing others into the vindication-praise. The target (107) is summoning-praise and the coupling (112) is 'fearers-praise'. Manner (108) none; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent; no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) at v23 shows the rescued interior widening the circle — it recruits the whole God-fearing community. Role (115) is characteristic. The process moves outward: an inner deliverance becomes a will to gather other reverent hearts into shared praise; here 'fear' functions almost as a name for the worshipping people.
narratives.story: Rescued, the psalmist does not keep his relief private but turns and calls out to everyone who fears God: praise him, honour him, stand in awe. His deliverance becomes an act of will — a deliberate gathering of the reverent into one chorus. 'Those who fear the LORD' here simply means God's worshipping people, and the psalmist wants them all singing. The movement runs from his own inside outward, pulling a whole community into praise.
narratives.variation_note: Almost alone among the twenty-two readings of this word, #1 is tagged volition, not affect/disposition: the God-fearers are the object of a summons the rescued self issues, so 'fear' names the worshipping community being recruited rather than the psalmist's own reverence or a promised blessing.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'I will fear no evil' and the type (102) is affect. No source (103 absent) inside the verse; no seat (104 none) — the fearlessness is a whole-self state (locus 116 internal:ib-state). The bearer (105) is the psalmist; the operation (106) is fear dissolved by presence: even walking through the valley of the shadow of death, the self fears no evil, for God is with it. The target (107) is fearlessness and the coupling (112) is 'fear-no-evil'. Manner (108) none; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent; no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) at v4 stresses that the darkest passage is faced without dread because of felt companionship. Role (115) is characteristic. The inner process is not the absence of danger but the neutralizing of its terror: the objective threat (deepest darkness) remains, yet the accompanying presence empties it of dread.
narratives.story: Walking through the darkest, most death-shadowed place, the psalmist says he will fear no evil — not because the danger is gone but because God is right there with him. The threat is real; what is missing is the terror it would normally bring. This calm is not felt in one organ but steadies the whole person. Nearness, not safety, is what dissolves the fear.
narratives.variation_note: Among the nineteen readings of this word, #1 is fearlessness produced specifically by God's companionship in mortal danger (coupling fear-no-evil), not by God's kingship, judgment, or a blessing — the threat stays and only the dread is emptied.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'the God-fearer instructed' and the type (102) is affect. No source (103 absent); no seat (104 none) — reverence is a whole-self posture (locus 116 internal:ib-state). The bearer (105) is 'the one who fears the LORD'; the operation (106) ties reward to reverence: whoever fears the LORD, God will instruct in the way he should choose. The target (107) is reverent-teachability and the coupling (112) is 'fearer-instructed'. Manner (108) none; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent; no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) at v12 makes reverence the condition of guidance — the fearing interior is the one God teaches which road to take. Role (115) is characteristic. The process runs from an inner posture (fear) to a divine response (instruction): the reverent self is rendered teachable, and its choosing is directed from outside itself.
narratives.story: The psalm asks who the God-fearing person is, and answers that God himself will teach such a person which way to go. Reverence for God is what makes someone open to that teaching. It is a settled attitude of the whole self, not a passing feeling. Because he fears God, he is guided in his choices — his reverence draws down instruction.
narratives.variation_note: Reading #2 links reverence to being taught the right way (target reverent-teachability) — fear as the condition of divine guidance — distinct from the many readings where the same word marks the recipients of God's love, provision, or blessing.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'the friendship of the LORD' and the type (102) is affect. No source (103 absent); no seat (104 none) — intimacy is a whole-self condition (locus 116 internal:ib-state). The bearer (105) is 'those who fear him'; the operation (106) is a shared secret: the intimate friendship and counsel of the LORD is for those who fear him, to whom he makes known his covenant. The target (107) is intimacy and the coupling (112) is 'friendship-with-God'. Manner (108) none; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent; no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) at v14 names it as admission to God's confidence — the God-fearing interior is told his secret. Role (115) is characteristic. The inner-being process turns reverence into relationship: fear, far from keeping God at a distance, becomes the doorway into closeness, the reverent self being drawn into a confided-in intimacy.
narratives.story: To those who fear him, God gives something surprising: his friendship. He lets them in on his secret and shares his covenant with them. Far from holding them at arm's length, reverence for God opens the door to real closeness. This intimacy belongs to the whole person's standing before God, and it is the reward of a fearing heart.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'whom shall I fear' and the type (102) is affect. No source (103 absent) inside the verse; no seat (104 none) — the fearlessness is a whole-self state (locus 116 internal:ib-state). The bearer (105) is the psalmist; the operation (106) is fear dissolved by who God is: with the LORD as light, salvation and stronghold, the self asks whom it should fear. The target (107) is fearlessness and the coupling (112) is 'whom-shall-I-fear'. Manner (108) none; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent; no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) at v1 shows fear cancelled at its root — the interior finds no ground for dread once God is its light. Role (115) is characteristic. The process is not resistance to fear but the removal of its foundation: a rhetorical question that expects the answer 'no one', because the character of God leaves the self no object worth dreading.
narratives.story: With God as his light, his rescue, and his fortress, the psalmist asks: so whom should I fear? The question expects the answer 'no one'. This is not fear fought off but fear left with nothing to stand on — once God is everything to him, no threat is big enough to dread. The calm belongs to the whole man, a settled confidence rather than a bodily reflex.
narratives.variation_note: Reading #2 grounds fearlessness in God's very identity as light, salvation and stronghold (coupling whom-shall-I-fear), so fear is cancelled at its root rather than merely refused mid-danger as in #1 (Psa 23:4).

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'terror on every side, they plot my life' and the type (102) is affect. No source (103 absent) is separately tagged and no seat (104 none) — the dread grips the whole self (locus 116 internal:ib-state), not one organ. The bearer (105) is the psalmist; the operation (106) is the dread of an encircling conspiracy: the self hears the whispering of many, terror on every side, as they scheme and plot to take its life. The target (107) is encircled-dread and the coupling (112) is 'terror-on-every-side'. Manner (108) none; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent; no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) at v13 shows the interior feeling the net of conspiracy closing. Role (115) characteristic. Here the fear-cluster is read at its dark pole: this is not reverence but raw terror, the inner being registering surrounding malice as a pressure it cannot escape — fear as siege.
narratives.story: The psalmist hears people whispering all around him, plotting to kill him, and terror closes in from every direction. This is not awe of God but pure dread — the feeling of a trap tightening. It seizes the whole man, not just one part of him. He senses enemies on all sides scheming, and the fear of that encircling malice presses in on him.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'goodness stored for those who fear you' and the type (102) is affect. No source (103 absent); no seat (104 none) — reverent trust is a whole-self posture (locus 116 internal:ib-state). The bearer (105) is 'those who fear him'; the operation (106): the self marvels at the abundant goodness God has stored up for those who fear him and take refuge in him — reverent trust and its treasured reward. The target (107) is reverent-refuge and the coupling (112) is 'goodness-stored'. Manner (108) none; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent; no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) at v19 names the interior posture (fear + refuge) that God secretly rewards with hoarded good. Role (115) characteristic. The process pairs two inner movements — reverence and taking-refuge — and links them to a stored, hidden reward; the fearing self is the one for whom God quietly keeps a treasury of goodness.
narratives.story: In the middle of trouble the psalmist suddenly marvels at how much good God has piled up in reserve for the people who fear him and run to him for shelter. Reverence and taking refuge go together, and God's answer to them is a hidden store of goodness kept ready. This is a settled orientation of the whole person, not a fleeting feeling. The fearing, sheltering heart is the one for whom God secretly treasures up good things.
narratives.variation_note: Reading #3 pairs reverence with taking-refuge and attaches it to God's stored-up, hidden reward (coupling goodness-stored) — fear as trusting dependence rewarded, distinct from readings where the same word marks reverence owed or the community summoned to praise.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'the fear God's eye rests on' and the type (102) is affect. No source (103 absent); no seat (104 none) — reverence is a whole-self state (locus 116 internal:ib-state). The bearer (105) is 'those who fear him'; the operation (106): the eye of the LORD is on those who fear him — reverent fear as the posture God watches over. The target (107) is reverent-fear and the coupling (112) is 'eye-on-the-fearing'. Manner (108) none; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent; no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) at v18 names the fearing interior as the one God keeps in view; reverence draws his watchful care. Role (115) characteristic. The inner process here is receptive rather than active: the self's reverence is the thing that attracts God's protective gaze, set against the vanity of horses and armies — the fearing heart is watched, not the strong arm.
narratives.story: Against the useless confidence of war-horses and great armies, the psalm says God's eye is fixed on those who fear him and hope in his love. Reverence is what draws God's watchful, caring attention. It is a settled attitude of the whole self. The fearing heart, not human strength, is what God keeps his eye on.
narratives.variation_note: Reading #4 casts reverence as the posture that attracts God's watchful eye (coupling eye-on-the-fearing), a receptive being-watched — different from #2 (taught) or #3 (rewarded with stored good): here the fruit of fear is simply God's protective gaze.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'fear the LORD, you his saints' and the type (102) is affect. No source (103 absent); no seat (104 none) — reverence is a whole-self posture (locus 116 internal:ib-state). The bearer (105) is 'the saints'; the operation (106): the self calls the saints to fear the LORD, for those who fear him have no lack — reverent fear that wants nothing. The target (107) is reverent-fear and the coupling (112) is 'fear-no-lack'. Manner (108) none; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent; no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) at v9 commends reverence as the interior posture that is fully supplied. Role (115) characteristic. The process is hortatory: an inner state (reverence) is urged on others with a promise attached — those who hold it lack nothing. Fear here is invitation, not terror, and it is bound to sufficiency.
narratives.story: The psalmist urges God's holy people to fear the LORD, promising that those who do will lack nothing. This is reverence held out as an invitation, not a threat. It is a settled attitude of the whole person, and it comes with a guarantee: the God-fearing want for nothing. Fear him, he says, and you will be fully supplied.
narratives.variation_note: Reading #3 is a call to others to fear God tied to the promise of no lack (coupling fear-no-lack) — reverence as invitation-with-sufficiency, distinct from the fearlessness readings (#1, #2) of the same word where the psalmist refuses dread.

narratives.narrative: Here the row-set is fuller. The sense (101) is 'fear / be afraid (yare, negated)' and the type (102) is action. Distinctively a source (103) IS present: the fearlessness is 'grounded in God our refuge and strength (v1)' — a pairing across spans that supplies the ground the earlier readings left absent. No seat (104 none). The bearer (105) is the people ('we'); the operation (106) is fear, negated. The target (107) is none — there is no object the fear settles on, because it is refused. The manner (108) is vivid: 'though the earth give way'. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent. The coupling (112) is none, but the prohibition (113) is explicit — negated: 'therefore we will NOT fear'. The discovery (114) makes it cosmic: fearlessness even at the collapse of creation, confidence grounded not in stability but in God as refuge. Role (115) characteristic; locus (116) internal:ib-state. The inner process is a communal 'we' refusing fear at the very shaking of the world, and — unusually — the verse names why: God is refuge and strength.
narratives.story: Even if the whole earth were to give way and the mountains crash into the sea, the community says together: we will not be afraid. This time the reason is stated outright — God is their refuge and strength. Their fearlessness is not built on things staying steady but on God himself, so it holds even as creation itself buckles. The threat is imagined at its most total, and still they refuse to be shaken.
narratives.variation_note: Reading #4 is the only reading of this word with an explicit source named (God as refuge, v1) and an explicit negated prohibition; its bearer is a communal 'we', not the lone psalmist, and its fearlessness is pitched at cosmic collapse — the ground of courage is spelled out rather than left implicit as in #1-#3.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'fear / revere (yare - to be feared)' and — notably — the type (102) is status: fear here is a property owed, not an act performed. No source (103 absent); no seat (104 none). The bearer (105) is 'all peoples' who owe him fear. The operation (106) is marked none — there is no interior event narrated, because the verse states a standing fact rather than a movement. The target (107) is 'the LORD Most High' and the locus (116) is external:god — the fear is oriented outward toward God, not held as an inner state. Manner (108) none; coupling (112) none; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111), prohibition (113) all absent. The discovery (114) names the reverent awe owed the great King, joy and fear together. Role (115) characteristic. The inner-being reading is subtle: the human faculty here is obligation — all peoples stand under a claim to revere the universal King; the psalm's shout of joy rests on this owed awe.
narratives.story: The LORD Most High is a great king over all the earth, and he is to be feared. This is not something the psalmist works up inside himself but a plain fact about God: every people owes him reverence. The awe is aimed outward at God, the rightful object of the whole earth's fear. And in this psalm that fear sits happily alongside shouting and clapping — awe and joy belong together before the great King.
narratives.variation_note: Reading #5 is tagged status with operation 'none' and locus external:god: fear as an obligation owed the universal King, not an inner event — unlike the fearlessness readings (#1, #2, #4) where the same word names the psalmist's own refused dread held as an internal state.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'trembling (raad)' and the type (102) is status. No source (103 absent); no seat (104 none) — the shudder grips the whole self (locus 116 internal:ib-state). The bearer (105) is 'the kings' — enemy rulers, not the psalmist. The operation (106) is 'take hold of them' (inferred): trembling seizes them. The target (107) is 'the kings' — they are the ones gripped. Manner (108) none; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent; no prohibition (113). The coupling (112) pairs the trembling 'with anguish' across spans — physical terror welded to inner pain. The discovery (114) reads it as the body registering the soul's dread: raad is the shuddering that grips the fleeing kings. Role (115) characteristic. Read without valence-bias, this is the interior of God's enemies: the mighty are seized by a bodily terror that betrays a collapsing inner state, awe's dark counterpart falling on the proud.
narratives.story: When the enemy kings saw Zion, panic took them: they trembled and fled, gripped like a woman in labour. The shaking is in the body, but it comes straight from a soul overwhelmed with dread and anguish. This is the inside of God's enemies at the moment their confidence breaks — the strong reduced to shuddering. Their bodies shake because their courage has given way.
narratives.variation_note: Reading #1 of this trembling-word falls on enemy kings as terror at God's power (bearer the kings, coupled with anguish); #2 (Psa 55:5) puts the identical trembling on the psalmist himself under the terrors of death — the same bodily dread, but seizing the foe here versus the sufferer there.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'be afraid (yare, negated)' and the type (102) is action. No source (103 absent); no seat (104 none) — the counsel addresses a whole-self attitude (locus 116 internal:ib-state). The bearer (105) is 'the hearer' being counselled; the operation (106) is 'be afraid', deprecated. The target (107) is the circumstance 'when a man becomes rich'. Manner (108) none; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent. The coupling (112) is none, but the prohibition (113) is explicit — deprecated: 'Be NOT afraid when a man becomes rich'. The discovery (114) reads it as counsel against dread or envy of the wealthy, since the rich carry nothing away in death. Role (115) characteristic. The inner-being process is corrective: a fear/anxiety that would naturally rise at another's growing wealth and power is named and forbidden, defused by the reminder of death's leveling — the self is told not to let riches intimidate it.
narratives.story: Don't be afraid, the psalm says, when someone grows rich and his household becomes ever more splendid. The dread or envy that wealth and power stir up is named and waved off. Why? Because when he dies he takes none of it with him — his glory will not follow him down. So the fear that riches try to press on the heart is simply forbidden as groundless.
narratives.variation_note: Reading #2 is an instructional 'be not afraid' aimed at anxiety over another's wealth (target 'when a man becomes rich'), a deprecated prohibition — unlike #1's personal refusal of battle-fear or #3-#5's trust-driven fearlessness; here the fear defused is intimidation by riches.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'fear (yare, rhetorical negation)' and the type (102) is action. No source (103 absent); no seat (104 none) — the refused fear is a whole-self attitude (locus 116 internal:ib-state). The bearer (105) is the psalmist; the operation (106) is fear, rhetorically none. The target (107) — via a span-pairing — is 'the cheaters' iniquity' that surrounds him. The manner (108) is 'in times of trouble'. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent; coupling (112) none. The prohibition (113) is 'rhetorically none' — 'Why should I fear?'. The discovery (114) reads it as fearlessness before the wealthy oppressor, since the rich cannot ransom themselves from death. Role (115) characteristic. The inner process is a reasoned refusal: hemmed in by the malice of the rich, the self asks why it should fear, and the psalm's whole argument (death undoes wealth) supplies the answer — dread of the powerful is unfounded.
narratives.story: Ringed by the wrongdoing of those who cheat him, the psalmist asks himself a pointed question: why should I be afraid, even in bad times? The answer runs through the whole psalm — the rich cannot buy their way out of death, so their power is not worth dreading. His fear of these oppressors is set aside by clear thinking, not just brushed off. Trouble presses in, and still he sees no reason to be afraid.
narratives.variation_note: Reading #6 is a rhetorical 'why should I fear?' aimed at wealthy oppressors in trouble (target the cheaters' iniquity), reasoned away by death's leveling of the rich — a thought-out refusal, paired later in the psalm with #2's 'be not afraid when a man becomes rich'.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'be brought forth / born (chul - in iniquity)' and the type (102) is status — a condition, not an act. No source (103 absent); no seat (104 none) — this sinfulness marks the whole self from its origin (locus 116 internal:ib-state). The bearer (105) is 'the penitent (from birth)'; the operation (106) is 'brought forth / born'. The target (107) is none — birth has no object it acts upon. The manner (108) is a span-pair: 'in iniquity, from conception'. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent; no prohibition (113). The coupling (112) welds it to 'in sin did my mother conceive me'. The discovery (114) reads it as the confession of innate, lifelong sinfulness — guilt not as an episode but as the human condition from the womb, the deepest layer of the penitent's self-knowledge. Role (115) characteristic. The inner-being process is self-recognition at the root: the interior traces its own corruption back before memory, to birth itself.
narratives.story: In his confession David digs beneath the single act of sin to something older: he says he was sinful from the moment he was born, that in guilt his mother conceived him. This is not blaming his mother but owning that his corruption is not a passing episode but the very condition he came into the world with. It marks the whole person, not one part, and reaches back before he could remember. It is the deepest thing he knows about himself as he begs for a clean heart.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'fear / be in awe (yare - see and fear)' and the type (102) is status. No source (103 absent); no seat (104 none). The bearer (105) is 'the righteous'; the operation (106) is 'fear / stand in awe'. The target (107) is 'at God's judgment', and the locus (116) is external:god — the awe is oriented toward God's act, not held as a private inner mood. Manner (108) none; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent; no prohibition (113). The coupling (112) pairs this awe, across spans, with 'the derisive laugh at the fallen tyrant'. The discovery (114) reads it as the reverent fear that seeing God cut down the mighty produces — sobering the onlookers before it turns to laughter. Role (115) characteristic. The inner process is a two-beat response: the righteous watch God topple the boastful oppressor, and their interior first registers awe, then derision — reverence and mockery held together as the fitting reaction to divine justice.
narratives.story: When the righteous watch God cut down the boastful tyrant who trusted in his wealth, their first reaction is awe — a sobered fear before God's justice. Then that awe tips into laughter at the fallen man who would not make God his refuge. The awe is aimed at what God has done, not at some feeling inside them. Seeing evil undone leaves them both reverent and, in the end, scornful of the ruin the wicked brought on himself.
narratives.variation_note: Reading #7 is awe at God's judgment on the tyrant (locus external:god), coupled with derisive laughter — reverence stirred by watching justice done, unlike the fearlessness readings (#1, #2, #6) or the reverence-owed reading (#5) of this same word.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'be in dread / terror (pachad - in great terror)' and the type (102) is status. Distinctively a source (103) is present: the terror comes 'because God scatters the bones of the besieger (v5)' — the dread is grounded in God's act. No seat (104 none). The bearer (105) is 'the evildoers'; the operation (106) is 'be seized with dread' (inferred). The target (107) is none — the terror has no object it reaches toward; it simply overtakes them. The manner (108) is a span-pair: 'great, such as has never been'. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent; coupling (112) none; no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) reads it as sudden, groundless dread overtaking the godless: those who feared nothing (the fool who says 'there is no God') are seized by unprecedented fear. Role (115) characteristic; locus (116) internal:ib-state. Read without valence-bias, this is the interior of the wicked collapsing: confident godlessness inverted into panic by God's intervention.
narratives.story: The fool had said in his heart there is no God and lived without any fear — until, suddenly, he is overwhelmed by terror greater than any before. The dread has a cause: God scatters the forces of those who came against his people. The panic seizes the whole man from within, out of nowhere as far as he can tell. Those who feared nothing are the very ones broken by unheard-of fear.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'terrors (emah - the terrors of death)' and the type (102) is status. No source (103 absent); no seat (104 none) — the dread presses on the whole self (locus 116 internal:ib-state). The bearer (105) is the psalmist; the operation (106) is 'fall upon him' (inferred) — the terrors descend like a weight. The target (107) is the psalmist himself — he is what they fall on. The manner (108) is a span-pair: 'of death'. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent; no prohibition (113). The coupling (112) welds it, across spans, to 'fear, trembling, horror (v5)'. The discovery (114) reads emah as the death-fear that descends on the betrayed man — the deepest layer of his anguish, opening onto fear and trembling. Role (115) characteristic. The inner-being process is invasion: an outer crisis (betrayal, enemy pressure) sinks to its lowest point as the dread of dying settles on the self and unfolds into a whole cascade of terror.
narratives.story: At the bottom of the psalmist's anguish lies the dread of death itself, which falls on him like a crushing weight. This is not reverence but raw terror, and it is the deepest layer of his distress — and it does not come alone. It opens out into fear, trembling, and horror that overwhelm him. Betrayed and pressed by enemies, he feels the very terror of dying settle over his whole being.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'fear / dread (yirah - fear and trembling come on me)' and the type (102) is status. No source (103 absent); no seat (104 none) — the dread floods the whole self (locus 116 internal:ib-state). The bearer (105) is the psalmist; the operation (106) is 'come upon him' (inferred). The target (107) is none — the fear has no object; it simply arrives and engulfs. Manner (108) none; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent; no prohibition (113). The coupling (112) pairs it, across spans, with 'trembling and horror'. The discovery (114) is decisive: yirah here is not reverence but raw terror, the first of the triad (fear, trembling, horror) that engulfs the psalmist under the death-terrors. Role (115) characteristic. The inner process is inundation — a fear that is not directed and not chosen but suffered, the reverence-word bent to name naked panic.
narratives.story: Fear and trembling come over the psalmist, and horror covers him. This is the very word often used for reverence, but here it means naked terror — dread that simply floods in, with nothing he can aim it at or do about it. It is the first of a rush of feelings that swallow him whole. Under the shadow of death and betrayal, the whole man is overtaken by panic he did not choose.
narratives.variation_note: Reading #2 bends this reverence-word to raw, undirected terror flooding the psalmist (paired with trembling and horror) — the opposite pole from #1 (clean, eternal fear of the LORD), #3-#5 (reverence owed / wisdom's start / the promise's aim). Same word, ascent to descent.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'trembling (raad - fear and trembling)' and the type (102) is status. No source (103 absent); no seat (104 none) — the shudder seizes the whole self (locus 116 internal:ib-state). The bearer (105) is the psalmist; the operation (106) is 'come upon him' (inferred). The target (107) is none — the trembling simply arrives. Manner (108) none; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent; no prohibition (113). The coupling (112) pairs it, across spans, with 'fear'. The discovery (114) reads raad as the body's share in the soul's dread — the physical trembling that terror produces, the outward tremor of inward fear. Role (115) characteristic. The inner-being process is the somatic overflow of terror: the same panic named as fear in the paired verse now shows in the body's shaking — inner dread made visible as a tremor the self cannot still.
narratives.story: Along with fear, trembling comes over the psalmist — his body shakes because his soul is overwhelmed with dread. The trembling is the outward sign of the terror within; the fear inside spills over into a shaking he cannot control. It simply comes upon him, unbidden. The panic of a man facing death and betrayal registers right down to his trembling limbs.
narratives.variation_note: Reading #2 of this trembling-word puts the shudder on the psalmist himself under death's terrors (paired with 'fear'), where #1 (Psa 48:6) put the same trembling on fleeing enemy kings — the identical bodily dread, borne by the sufferer here rather than the foe.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'fear (yare - do not fear God)' and the type (102) is status. A source (103) is present: 'so God will give ear and humble them (v19)' — the enemies' fearlessness is what draws God's humbling response. No seat (104 none). The bearer (105) is 'the enemies (lacking it)' — this is fear defined by its absence in the wicked. The operation (106) is 'do not fear' (inferred). The target (107) is God, and the locus (116) is external:god. Manner (108) none; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent; no prohibition (113). The coupling (112) pairs it, across spans, with 'their refusal to change'. The discovery (114) reads their fearlessness as the root of their obstinacy — the same godlessness as the ruthless and the fool. Role (115) characteristic. Read without valence-bias, the inner-being process is a missing faculty: the enemies' lack of reverence for God underlies their refusal to change, and precisely that absence provokes God to answer and bring them low.
narratives.story: The psalmist's enemies never change their ways, and the reason is plain: they do not fear God. Their refusal to reform and their lack of reverence are the same thing — the settled godlessness that also marks the fool and the ruthless. And that very absence of fear is what moves God to hear and humble them. Here the point is not fear present but fear missing, and the ruin that missing fear invites.
narratives.variation_note: Reading #8 is defined by absent reverence in the enemies (bearer 'the enemies lacking it', locus external:god), its lack coupled to their refusal to change and drawing God's humbling — unlike the psalmist's own refused battle-fear (#1, #6) or reverence owed (#5): here fear's absence is the finding.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'be afraid (yare - I shall not be afraid)' and the type (102) is status. No source (103 absent); no seat (104 none) — the fearlessness is a whole-self state (locus 116 internal:ib-state). The bearer (105) is the psalmist; the operation (106) is 'not be afraid' (inferred). The target (107) is none — the fear is refused, so it settles on nothing. Manner (108) none; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent; no prohibition (113). The coupling (112) marks it as 'the fearlessness of v4 restated'. The discovery (114) reads it as fearlessness confirmed, yare negated a second time, now measured against 'man' rather than 'flesh' — mortal man reduced to no threat before the trusted God. Role (115) characteristic. The inner process is consolidation: the psalm's central movement (fear pivoting into trust) reaches a settled second statement, the self rehearsing its confidence so that dread of human enemies is emptied.
narratives.story: 'I shall not be afraid,' the psalmist says again; 'what can man do to me?' This repeats and confirms the confidence he first reached earlier in the psalm. Measured against God, mortal man shrinks to no real threat at all. The calm belongs to the whole person, a settled trust rather than a passing feeling. Having once turned his fear into trust, he now states his fearlessness a second time, firmly.
narratives.variation_note: Among the eight readings of 'afraid', #3 is the settled restatement (coupling 'fearlessness of v4 restated') of trust-won calm, measured against 'man' — the resolved end of the fear-to-trust movement, distinct from #4 (fear frankly owned) and #5 (fear first overcome).

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'be afraid (yare - when I am afraid)' and the type (102) is status. No source (103 absent); no seat (104 none) — the fear is a whole-self state (locus 116 internal:ib-state). The bearer (105) is the psalmist; the operation (106) is 'be afraid' (inferred) — here fear is owned, not refused. The target (107) is none. Manner (108) none; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent; no prohibition (113). The coupling (112) is decisive: the fear is 'answered by trust in the same breath'. The discovery (114) names this the psalm's key hinge — fear frankly owned, not denied, pivoting directly into trust, the movement the whole psalm turns on. Role (115) characteristic. The inner-being process is the pivot itself: honest fear does not paralyse but becomes the very occasion of trust — 'when I am afraid, I put my trust in you'. This is the most candid of the eight readings: dread admitted, then redirected.
narratives.story: 'When I am afraid,' the psalmist says plainly, 'I put my trust in you.' He does not pretend the fear away; he admits it honestly. But in the same breath the fear turns into trust — the admission itself becomes the doorway to confidence. This is the hinge the whole psalm swings on. His dread does not freeze him; it drives him straight to God.
narratives.variation_note: Reading #4 is unique among the eight 'afraid' readings for owning the fear rather than negating it (operation 'be afraid', coupled to trust in the same breath) — it is the psalm's hinge, where #3 and #5 are the resolved 'I shall not be afraid' that follows from it.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'be afraid (yare - I shall not be afraid)' and the type (102) is status. No source (103 absent); no seat (104 none) — the fearlessness is a whole-self state (locus 116 internal:ib-state). The bearer (105) is the psalmist; the operation (106) is 'not be afraid' (inferred). The target (107) is none. Manner (108) none; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent; no prohibition (113). The coupling (112) marks it as 'the fear of v3 now overcome by trust'. The discovery (114) reads it as fear conquered by trust — the fruit of trusting God's word, with mortal 'flesh' shrunk to nothing before the trusted God. Role (115) characteristic. The inner-being process is the immediate result of the pivot: having turned fear into trust in v3, the self now declares it will not be afraid; 'flesh' — mortal humanity — can do nothing to it. The measure here is 'flesh', which #3 later restates as 'man'.
narratives.story: Right after admitting his fear, the psalmist declares the result: because he trusts God's word, he will not be afraid — for what can mere flesh do to him? The dread he owned a moment before is now overcome. Weighed against the God he trusts, frail human enemies come to nothing. His fearlessness here is the direct fruit of the trust he just reached.
narratives.variation_note: Reading #5 is the first 'I shall not be afraid' (coupling 'fear of v3 overcome by trust'), measured against 'flesh' — the immediate fruit of the hinge in #4; #3 (v11) restates it against 'man'. Three beats of one movement: owned (#4), overcome (#5), restated (#3).

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'fear / revere (yare - those who fear you)' and the type (102) is status. A source (103) is present: the God-fearers are those 'whom God has disciplined by rejecting and breaking them (v1)' — reverence set against the backdrop of defeat. No seat (104 none). The bearer (105) is 'the God-fearing people'; the operation (106) is 'fear / revere God' (inferred). The target (107) is God, and the locus (116) is external:god. The manner (108) is 'fleeing to the banner God set up'. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent; no prohibition (113). The coupling (112) pairs them, across spans, with 'God's beloved (v5)'. The discovery (114) reads them as the reverent remnant given a rallying-point in defeat — disciplined yet given a banner to flee to. Role (115) characteristic. The inner-being process is corporate reverence under discipline: a people rejected and broken by God still bear the mark of fearing him, and to that fearing remnant God gives a banner, a place to regroup.
narratives.story: God has rejected his people and broken their defences, yet even in that defeat there is a company who still fear him — and for them he raises a banner to rally to, a place to flee from the enemy's bow. These same God-fearers are the ones he loves and will save. Their reverence stands out precisely against the backdrop of discipline and loss. Fearing God marks the remnant he still gathers when everything else has fallen.
narratives.variation_note: Reading #5 places the God-fearers in a scene of national defeat (source: rejected and broken, v1), reverence as the mark of the disciplined remnant given a banner — distinct from readings where fear is rewarded with provision or love: here it is fear that survives God's own chastening.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'dwell / sojourn (gur - let me dwell in your tent)' and the type (102) is action. No source (103 absent); no seat (104 none) — the longing is a whole-self orientation, though the locus (116) here is external:god, fixed on God's dwelling. The bearer (105) is the psalmist; the operation (106) is 'dwell / abide'. The target (107), via span-pairing, is 'in God's tent, forever', and the manner (108) is 'forever'. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent; no prohibition (113). The coupling (112) pairs it, across spans, with 'taking refuge under his wings'. The discovery (114) reads it as the longing for permanent nearness to God — not a fugitive's brief shelter but a settled home in his presence, forever. Role (115) characteristic. The inner-being process is desire reoriented: the same word that elsewhere means the exile's precarious sojourn is turned into a positive craving to be God's abiding guest, dwelling and sheltering as one continuous longing.
narratives.story: From the end of the earth the psalmist cries out one deep wish: to live in God's tent forever, to take shelter under the covering of his wings. The word for a stranger's temporary stay is turned here into a longing for a permanent home — not a brief hideout but a settled place in God's presence for good. Dwelling with God and hiding under his wings are the same desire. His whole heart reaches toward lasting nearness to God.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'fear / revere (yare - those who fear your name)' and the type (102) is status. No source (103 absent); no seat (104 none). The bearer (105) is 'those who fear God's name'; the operation (106) is 'fear / revere' (inferred). The target (107), via span-pairing, is 'God's name', and the locus (116) is external:god. Manner (108) none; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent; no prohibition (113). The coupling (112) pairs them, across spans, as 'the company whose heritage the psalmist is given'. The discovery (114) reads it as the psalmist counted among the God-fearing — belonging to the fearing community is itself the gift. Role (115) characteristic. The inner-being process is one of belonging: the psalmist is granted 'the heritage of those who fear your name', so reverence functions here as membership — the fearing community is a body whose inheritance the self is glad to share.
narratives.story: The psalmist rejoices that God has given him the inheritance that belongs to those who fear his name. To fear God is to belong to a community, and being counted among them is itself the gift he celebrates. Their reverence is aimed at God's name, and the psalmist is glad to be numbered with them. Membership in the God-fearing company is treated as a treasured heritage.
narratives.variation_note: Reading #6 uses the word for belonging — the psalmist granted the heritage of the God-fearers (coupled as the company whose heritage he shares) — reverence as membership in a community, distinct from readings where fear draws provision, guidance, or love to the fearer individually.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'dread / terror (pachad - dread of the enemy)' and the type (102) is status. No source (103 absent); no seat (104 none) — the dread grips the whole self (locus 116 internal:ib-state). The bearer (105) is the psalmist; the operation (106) is 'be in dread' (inferred). The target (107) is 'of the enemy'. Manner (108) none; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent; no prohibition (113). The coupling (112) marks it as 'the fear that drives the complaint'. The discovery (114) reads pachad as the fear of the hidden foe, from which the psalmist begs preservation — the anxiety of one shot at from ambush. Role (115) characteristic. The inner-being process is the terror that launches the prayer: the psalmist opens by asking God to guard his life from the dread of the enemy, so this fear is not refused but voiced as the very pressure driving him to cry out.
narratives.story: The psalm opens with the psalmist begging God to protect his life from the dread of the enemy. This is the fear of a hidden, plotting foe — the anxiety of a man who feels himself aimed at from ambush. He does not deny the fear; he names it as the thing pushing him to pray. The whole complaint rises out of this dread of secret enemies.
narratives.variation_note: Reading #1 of this dread-word is the psalmist's own fear of a hidden enemy, the anxiety that opens and drives the psalm (target 'of the enemy'); #2 (Psa 105:38) puts the same dread on the Egyptians toward Israel — the sufferer's fear here versus the oppressor's fear there.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'fear (yare - shooting without fear)' and the type (102) is status. No source (103 absent); no seat (104 none) — the missing fear is a whole-self trait (locus 116 internal:ib-state). The bearer (105) is 'the wicked (lacking it)'; the operation (106) is 'shoot without fear' (inferred). The target (107) is none. Manner (108) none; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent; no prohibition (113). The coupling (112) marks it as 'the brazenness of their ambush'. The discovery (114) reads yare as negated in the wicked — they shoot with no fear of God or reckoning, the same godless boldness as those who ask 'who will see us?'. Role (115) characteristic. Read without valence-bias, the inner-being process is a defiant absence: the wicked's lack of any fear of God frees them to loose their arrows at the innocent suddenly and shamelessly — malice unrestrained precisely because reverence is missing.
narratives.story: The wicked take aim at the blameless and shoot suddenly, without any fear. What is missing in them is the very thing that would hold them back — a fear of God, any thought that they will be called to account. Because they dread nothing, they act with brazen boldness, sure no one will see or judge them. Here the point is the absence of fear, and how that absence sets malice loose.
narratives.variation_note: Reading #9 is fear absent in the wicked (bearer 'the wicked lacking it'), whose fearlessness enables their brazen ambush — the dark counterpart to the psalmist's God-grounded fearlessness (#1, #2); here missing fear frees malice rather than steadying trust.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'fear / stand in awe (yare - then all mankind fears)' and the type (102) is status. No source (103 absent); no seat (104 none). The bearer (105) is 'all mankind'; the operation (106) is 'fear / stand in awe'. The target (107) is 'at God's judgment', and the locus (116) is external:god. Manner (108) none; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent; no prohibition (113). The coupling (112) marks that it 'issues in telling and pondering God's deed'. The discovery (114) reads it as awe replacing the wicked's fearlessness — the fear the enemies lacked (v4) now falling on everyone who sees God's work. Role (115) characteristic. The inner-being process is a reversal and a spread: the very reverence the plotters refused (#9) now overtakes all mankind when God turns the wicked's arrows back on them, and this awe does not stay silent but issues in telling and pondering what God has done.
narratives.story: When God suddenly turns the wicked's own weapons back on them, everyone who sees it is struck with awe. The fear the plotters would not feel now falls on all mankind. And this awe does not fall silent — people tell what God has done and think hard about it. Human dread, refused by the wicked, comes back around to grip the whole watching world when God's justice is displayed.
narratives.variation_note: Reading #10 is the mirror of #9 in the same psalm: the fear the wicked lacked (v4) now seizes all mankind at God's judgment (locus external:god), issuing in proclamation — awe restored and spread, where #9 was awe defiantly absent.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'be in awe / fear (yare)' and the type (102) is status. A source (103) is present: the awe rises 'at God who established the mountains and stills the seas (v6-7)'. No seat (104 none). The bearer (105) is 'those who dwell at the ends of the earth'; the operation (106) is 'be in awe / stand in fear'. The target (107), via span-pairing, is 'at God's signs', and the locus (116) is external:god. Manner (108) none; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent; coupling (112) none; no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) reads it as reverent wonder at God's power over creation — the awe of the whole earth before the God who set the mountains and stilled the roaring seas and the tumult of peoples. Role (115) characteristic. The inner-being process is creation-wide wonder: the sight of God's control over nature and nations wakes reverent fear in people at the farthest edges of the world, awe as the fitting creaturely answer to the Creator's might.
narratives.story: People living at the very ends of the earth are filled with awe at the signs of God's power. What stirs them is the God who set the mountains in place, who quiets the roar of the seas and the uproar of the nations. Seeing his might over creation, they cannot help but stand in reverent wonder. Awe is the natural answer of the whole world to a Creator that strong.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'fear / revere (yare - all you who fear God)' and the type (102) is status. No source (103 absent); no seat (104 none). The bearer (105) is 'the God-fearing'; the operation (106) is 'fear / revere God' (inferred). The target (107) is God, and the locus (116) is external:god. Manner (108) none; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent; no prohibition (113). The coupling (112) marks them as 'the audience summoned to hear the testimony'. The discovery (114) reads them as the reverent community, the fit audience for testimony — those whose fear of God makes them able to receive and rejoice in what God has done for a fellow believer's soul. Role (115) characteristic. The inner-being process is receptive fellowship: the psalmist calls the God-fearing to come and hear what God has done for him, so reverence here qualifies people as the right hearers of another's testimony — a shared capacity to be glad at God's work in a neighbour.
narratives.story: 'Come and hear,' the psalmist says, 'all you who fear God, and I will tell what he has done for my soul.' Reverence for God is what makes people the right audience for such a story — they can take it in and rejoice in it. He gathers the God-fearing as fellow listeners to his testimony. Their shared fear of God makes them glad to hear what God has done for one of their own.
narratives.variation_note: Reading #7 casts the God-fearing as the fit audience for testimony (coupled as those summoned to hear), reverence as receptive fellowship — different from readings where fear draws reward to the fearer; here it qualifies the hearer to rejoice in another's rescue.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'fear / revere (yare - let all the ends of the earth fear him)' and the type (102) is status. A source (103) is present: reverence rises 'because God blesses us (v6-7)'. No seat (104 none). The bearer (105) is 'all the ends of the earth'; the operation (106) is 'fear / revere'. The target (107) is God, and the locus (116) is external:god. Manner (108) none; intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent; coupling (112) none; no prohibition (113). The discovery (114) reads it as reverent fear as the psalm's closing goal — the harvest and the blessing meant to turn the ends of the earth to fear and worship God. Role (115) characteristic. The inner-being process is blessing-driven reverence: God's gift (the yielded harvest, his blessing on his people) is meant to ripple outward so that the whole earth comes to fear him — awe as the intended harvest of grace, the psalm's final hope.
narratives.story: The psalm ends with a wish: that because God has blessed his people and the earth has yielded its harvest, all the ends of the earth would come to fear him. God's kindness is meant to spread outward until the whole world stands in awe of him. The blessing is not an end in itself but a means to draw every nation to reverence. That worldwide fear of God is the psalmist's closing hope.
narratives.variation_note: Reading #11 makes God's blessing the source and the whole earth's reverence the goal (source: because God blesses us) — awe as the intended fruit of grace spreading outward, distinct from readings where fear is the community's own settled trait or the enemies' missing faculty.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'fear / revere (yare - may they fear you while the sun endures)' and the type (102) is status. No source (103 absent); no seat (104 none). The bearer (105) is 'the people, throughout the reign'; the operation (106) is 'fear / revere God'. The target (107) is God, and the locus (116) is external:god. The manner (108) is 'while the sun endures, throughout all generations'. Intensity (109), specifier (110), effect (111) absent; no prohibition (113). The coupling (112) marks it as 'the reverence a righteous reign fosters'. The discovery (114) reads it as the enduring fear of God among the people under a just king — good government drawing hearts to worship, faith lasting as sun and moon. Role (115) characteristic. The inner-being process links political justice to reverence: under a king who judges rightly and defends the poor, the people's fear of God is sustained across generations, so righteous rule becomes the soil in which lasting reverence grows.
narratives.story: The prayer for the king is that under his just rule the people would go on fearing God as long as the sun and moon endure, through every generation. Good and righteous government is pictured as the very thing that keeps reverence alive in a people. Where the poor are defended and justice is done, hearts are drawn to worship God — and that fear lasts. The psalm ties the health of a nation's reverence to the justice of its ruler.
narratives.variation_note: Reading #12 ties reverence to the endurance of a righteous reign (manner: while the sun endures, all generations) — fear as the lasting fruit of just government, unlike readings where it responds to judgment or blessing; here it is sustained across generations by righteous rule.

narratives.narrative: The sense (101) is 'fear / be in awe (yare - the earth feared)' and — distinctively — the type (102) is response: fear as a reaction to a prior act. No source (103 absent) is separately tagged, though the trigger is named in the operation. No seat (104 none). The bearer (105) is 'the earth / its inhabitants'; the operation (106) is 'fear / be awestruck'. The target (107), via span-pairing, is 'God, who uttered judgment from heaven', and the locus (116) is external:god. The manner (108), via span-pairing, is 'struck silent'. It does not argue or cry out; it goes still. So complete is the dread before God's sentence that every voice on earth is hushed.

narratives.story: Because the people would not truly trust God, he let their days vanish like a breath and their years be swallowed up in terror. This is not a single scare but the whole texture of a life lived under judgment — years drained away, spent in dread. Their faithlessness led to a long, ambient fear coloring all their time. The terror here is the very condition of a wasted, futile life.

narratives.story: God led his people through the wilderness in safety, so that they were not afraid, while the same sea he parted for them drowned their enemies. Their calm was not their own doing but the fruit of being shepherded by God. Danger closed over the foe, yet his people walked on unafraid under his guidance. Their whole condition was one of security because of who was leading them.

Reverence for God is the settled inner posture that stands ready to receive his rescue. It is not fright but a leaning of the whole self toward God. To such fearing hearts, deliverance draws close.

narratives.story: 'Unite my heart to fear your name,' the psalmist prays. He knows his inner life is pulled in many directions, and he asks God to gather it into one — and the whole point of that wholeness is to fear and worship God single-mindedly. Reverence is the aim his prayer for an undivided heart is reaching toward. He wants to be made whole so that he can worship without distraction.

narratives.story: Reflecting on how briefly and heavily human life passes under God's displeasure, the psalmist notes that no one really grasps the power of God's anger, or fears him as much as he deserves to be feared. The reverence owed God outweighs what people actually give. Human fear falls short of the true weight of his wrath. The lament is partly that mankind does not fear God nearly enough.
narratives.variation_note: Reading #3 measures reverence by a shortfall — human fear falling short of what God's wrath deserves (coupled with considering his anger) — a sober deficit, unlike #1 (clean, eternal fear) or #4 (wisdom's beginning); here the finding is that mankind under-fears God.

narratives.story: The one who makes God his refuge will not be afraid of the terror that comes by night, or the arrow that flies by day, or the plague that stalks in the dark. Each real danger is named — and then refused. The fearlessness is not blindness to the threats but trust that God shelters him through them. Sheltered under God's wings, the trusting person meets a whole list of terrors without dread.
narratives.variation_note: Reading #15 is fearlessness defined against a named catalogue of terrors (night, arrow, plague), dread dissolved by God's shelter — where other 'fear' readings are reverence owed; this one is the sheltered person's refusal of specific fears.

Fear and adoration are one motion.
narratives.story: 'Worship the LORD in the splendour of holiness; tremble before him, all the earth.' The trembling called for here is not the shaking of terror but the awe that runs through true worship. To come before God rightly is to be moved to the point of trembling. The whole earth is summoned to bow and shake, its adoration and its holy fear inseparable.

narratives.story: 'The LORD reigns; let the peoples tremble!' Simply because God is king, enthroned above the cherubim, the nations are called to shake before him. Their inner trembling is matched by the earth itself quaking. This awe is not the fear of some particular danger but the response to sheer majesty — the presence of the reigning God is enough to make the whole world tremble.

narratives.story: When God rebuilds Zion and shows himself in his glory, the nations will come to fear his name and the kings of the earth will stand in awe of his splendour. The sight of God restoring his city and appearing in glory awakens reverence far beyond his own people. Peoples who did not fear him are drawn to awe by what he has visibly done. Reverence spreads as God's glory becomes plain to the world.
narratives.variation_note: Reading #16 has reverence spreading to the nations at God's visible restoration of Zion (paired with kings fearing his glory) — awe awakened by a manifested act, distinct from the settled covenant-community readings; here fear is the world's response to God's displayed glory.

narratives.story: As high as the sky is above the earth, the psalm says, so great is God's steadfast love toward those who fear him. Reverence for God is not met with distance but with immeasurable love. The fearing heart is exactly the one God floods with kindness. Far from holding people back, fearing God is the posture that draws down his boundless love.
narratives.variation_note: Reading #9 pairs reverence with the sky-high measure of God's steadfast love (coupled with his great steadfast love) — fear as the recipient of immeasurable love; #10 (v13) and #11 (v17) in the same cluster pair it with compassion and everlasting love, three facets of one truth.

narratives.story: Like a father who feels for his children, God shows tender compassion to those who fear him. The picture turns fear into something warm: the God-fearer is treated not as a frightened servant but as a beloved child. God knows how frail we are, that we are dust, and answers our reverence with a father's mercy. Fearing God and being cherished by him belong together.
narratives.variation_note: Reading #10 frames reverence in a father-child image (coupled with God's compassion), fear answered by fatherly tenderness — within the same Psa 103 cluster as #9 (steadfast love) and #11 (everlasting love), this facet stresses the intimacy of the fearer's relation to God.

narratives.story: Human life is fleeting — the wind blows over the flower and it is gone. But God's love, the psalm says, is from everlasting to everlasting on those who fear him, reaching down even to their children's children. Reverence for God links the frail, short-lived person to a love that never ends. Against the shortness of our days, the fearing heart rests in an unending love.

narratives.story: When God's people were still just a handful, they lived as strangers in the land that had been promised to them. They belonged to it by promise but were foreigners in it by fact — few, unsettled, wandering. This is the pilgrim condition: at home in what God has pledged, yet not at home in the world around them. The patriarchs held a land they did not yet possess.

narratives.story: Jacob and his family came down and lived as strangers in Egypt, the land of Ham. The pilgrim life that began with the patriarchs now carries on into a whole nation — a people dwelling in a country that is not their own. Even as they grow there, they remain resident aliens, at home nowhere but in God's promise. Their life as strangers is renewed a generation on.

narratives.story: After the plagues, Egypt was so filled with dread of Israel that it was glad to see them go. The nation that had enslaved them was now afraid of them. Their fear turned into relief at Israel's departure — they could not wait to be rid of the people they had oppressed. The powerful oppressor was reduced to terror of the ones he had held down.

narratives.story: The psalm reaches its high point with a famous line: the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom. Reverence for God is not just one good quality but the very foundation on which real wisdom and understanding are built. To know rightly, a person must first stand in awe of God. Everyone who lives by that reverence has good understanding.
narratives.variation_note: Reading #4 is the foundational claim — reverence as the beginning of wisdom (coupled with wisdom and understanding) — fear as the root of knowing rightly; distinct from #1 (fear as a clean possession), #3 (fear humans withhold), #5 (fear the promise aims at). Here it is the ground of all wisdom.

narratives.story: God gives food to those who fear him, the psalm says, and he never forgets his covenant with them. Reverence for God is met with steady, practical care — he feeds his people and keeps his promises to them. The fearing heart is not left to fend for itself but is provided for. Fearing God places a person within a relationship of dependable provision.
narratives.variation_note: Reading #12 links reverence to God's provision and kept covenant (coupled with provision and remembered covenant) — fear answered by concrete sustenance; distinct from #13 (v10, wisdom's beginning) in the same acrostic psalm: here the fearer is fed, there fear founds wisdom.

narratives.story: 'Blessed is the man who fears the LORD, who greatly delights in his commandments.' This reverence is the root from which the whole of the good man's life grows — his generosity, his steadiness, his fearlessness in bad times all spring from it. Fearing God and loving his commands are two sides of one settled attitude. Everything the psalm goes on to praise begins here, in the fear of the LORD.

The reverent disposition produces a steadiness that ill tidings cannot shake — fear of God crowding out fear of circumstance.
narratives.story: The man who fears the LORD is not afraid of bad news; his heart is steady, trusting in God. Precisely because he reveres God, other fears lose their grip on him — even a report of disaster cannot rattle him. His inner life is firm, anchored in trust. Fearing God has crowded out the fear of circumstances.

This second statement of his fearlessness turns from bad news to his human opponents. His reverence for God gives him a calm that outlasts every threat. He can face his foes without dread, sure of the outcome.

Fearing God and leaning on him are not opposites but partners; the very people who revere him are the ones urged to rely on him completely. Reverence naturally flows into confident trust.

Reverence for God is the one thing that matters here, and it draws down a blessing that reaches every rank alike, from the least to the greatest. Standing and status count for nothing; the fearing heart is what God blesses. His favour falls on all who revere him, high and low together.

Reverence for God here becomes a voice in a shared song, taking up the confession that God's love never ends. The God-fearing add their part to the chorus. Their fear finds expression as communal praise.

narratives.story: 'The LORD is on my side; I will not fear. What can man do to me?' Because God stands with him, the psalmist refuses to be afraid, and human enemies shrink to nothing. His calm rests not on how weak his foes are but on how sure he is of God's help. With God as his ally, the worst that people can do loses its power to frighten him.

narratives.story: 'Confirm to your servant your promise, that you may be feared,' the psalmist prays. He wants God to make good his word not merely for reassurance but so that his own reverence for God will grow. The surer he is of God's promise, the deeper his awe becomes. Reverence is the very thing the confirmed promise is meant to produce in him.
narratives.variation_note: Reading #5 makes reverence the goal a confirmed promise produces (target God's word) — fear as the intended fruit of assurance; distinct from #4 (wisdom's beginning) and #1 (clean, eternal fear): here the confirmed word deepens the servant's awe.

narratives.story: 'Take away the disgrace that I dread, for your laws are good,' the psalmist prays. Even this deeply devout man admits a real fear — the shame of being reproached — and he does not hide it. He brings the dread honestly to God and asks him to remove it. Loving God's word does not make him fearless; it gives him somewhere to bring his fear.

narratives.story: 'I am a friend to all who fear you, to those who keep your precepts,' the psalmist says. He knows who he is by the company he chooses — the people who revere God and obey his word. Reverence marks out a fellowship, and he counts himself firmly within it. Fearing God is a bond he shares with others, and he is glad to belong among them.
narratives.variation_note: Reading #18 locates reverence in chosen fellowship — the psalmist a companion of all who fear God (target God's word) — fear as shared identity, distinct from readings where fear draws blessing or provision; here it defines the company the self belongs to.

narratives.story: 'Those who fear you shall see me and rejoice, because I have hoped in your word.' When the God-fearing see how the psalmist has held on in hope, they are glad with him. Reverence binds them together, so that one person's trust becomes a shared joy. The same fellowship appears again a few verses later, when he asks that those who fear God would turn to him. Their shared reverence makes them rejoice in one another's faith.
narratives.variation_note: Reading #17 is reverence sharing in another's hope, the God-fearers rejoicing at the psalmist's trust (target God's word), and it recurs at v79 where he asks the same fearers to turn to him — one continuous reading; distinct from #16 (v4, the fearers voicing the antiphon of God's love).

narratives.story: 'My flesh trembles for fear of you; I am afraid of your judgments.' Here reverence is so intense it shakes the psalmist's very body — his skin creeps with awe of God. This is no calm, mild feeling but dread before God's judgments, gripping even a man who loves God's law. Awe of God can reach right down into the flesh and make it tremble.

narratives.story: In the same breath where his flesh trembles, the psalmist adds, 'and I am afraid of your judgments.' This is the mind's dread of God's justice matching the body's shaking. Two kinds of fear meet in one verse — the creeping of his skin and the fear in his thoughts before what God has decreed. The whole person, body and mind, stands in dread of God's judgments.

narratives.story: 'Princes persecute me without cause, but my heart stands in awe of your words.' Powerful men hound the psalmist for no reason, yet what truly grips his heart is not fear of them but awe of God's word. The reverence he feels for what God has said outweighs the threat of his persecutors. Awe of God's word steadies him against the fear of men.

The interior state is one of alienation and longing, the exile grieving that his dwelling is among the hostile.
narratives.story: 'Woe is me, that I dwell as a stranger in Meshech, among the tents of Kedar!' The psalmist grieves that he must live far from home among people who hate peace. Being a stranger here is not a neutral fact but a real distress — he feels the ache of exile among the hostile. His whole condition is one of alienation and longing to be somewhere better.

narratives.story: 'Blessed is everyone who fears the LORD, who walks in his ways.' The reverence praised here shows itself in ordinary living — in the paths a person walks and the work of their hands. Fearing God and walking in his ways are one and the same posture, and from it grows a fruitful, settled life. This is reverence lived out in everyday faithfulness.

narratives.story: 'This is how the man is blessed who fears the LORD.' After picturing the God-fearer's flourishing home and family, the psalm circles back to say plainly where it all comes from: the fear of the LORD. Reverence is named again as the single root of the whole blessing. Everything good in this life traces back to a heart that fears God.

The self that is forgiven does not grow careless but more reverent — God's mercy, rather than dissolving awe, is precisely what generates it. Out of the depths the psalmist finds that being forgiven binds him closer in reverent fear.
narratives.story: 'With you there is forgiveness, that you may be feared.' Strikingly, being pardoned does not make a person careless — it makes them revere God more. Mercy, not judgment, is what deepens awe here. The one lifted out of guilt does not take God lightly but holds him in greater reverence. Forgiveness itself is what produces the fear of God.
narratives.variation_note: Reading #19 is the paradox of the family: forgiveness itself produces reverence (target 'because there is forgiveness') — awe deepened by pardon, not dissolved by it; unlike readings where fear draws blessing, here mercy is the source that generates fear.

narratives.story: 'You who fear the LORD, bless the LORD!' Alongside Israel and the priestly houses, the God-fearing are called to praise God from Zion. Their reverence is precisely what fits them to bless him. Fear of God here flows straight into worship — those who stand in awe of him are the ones summoned to sing his praise. Reverence and praise are one act.
narratives.variation_note: Reading #20 summons the reverent to bless God (coupled with blessing him) — fear issuing in doxology, distinct from readings where the fearer receives blessing (Psa 115, 128); here the God-fearing are the ones who give praise.

Role (115) characteristic. The inner-being process is honest self-assessment as plea: rather than claim innocence, the self asks God not to bring it to trial, knowing it could not stand. Fear of God here takes the form of a sober knowledge of one's own unrighteousness.
narratives.story: 'Do not bring your servant into judgment, for no one alive is righteous before you.' The psalmist does not ask God for a fair trial — he knows he would lose. Instead of claiming to be innocent, he clearly sees and admits that no living person can stand as righteous before God. This honest, humbling self-knowledge becomes his plea. It is a kind of fear of God expressed as sober truth about himself.
narratives.variation_note: Reading #2 of 'enter' is tagged cognition, not affect: the psalmist's clear-eyed confession that none is righteous, a plea NOT to be entered into judgment — the reverse of #1 (Psa 5:7), where 'enter' was the reverent approach INTO God's house to worship. Approach to worship there, dread of a verdict here.

Role (115) characteristic. The inner-being process binds reverence to answered dependence: the fearing self is the one whose longings God satisfies and whose cries he answers. Fear here is not distance but a needy, trusting openness that God reliably meets — reverence as the posture God stoops to hear.
narratives.story: 'He fulfils the desire of those who fear him; he hears their cry and saves them.' Reverence for God is pictured here as a trusting dependence that God never leaves unanswered.
